site.title: Gordon Bailey — Internship Portfolio
site.lede: Everything built this summer, in one place. Four separate projects, one at each phase of the product development lifecycle, plus two side projects. UTM was the main one. Every page answers the same five questions: what the problem was, what I did, what came out of it, what it does not cover, and what to do next.

tracks.title: The product development lifecycle
tracks.blurb: Four different problems, four separate projects. Each sat at a different phase, so between them they cover the whole cycle.

tracks.title: Side projects
tracks.blurb: Neither was on anyone's roadmap. One came out of finding my feet, one out of curiosity.

_comment: One node per page. `parent` nests it; `order` sorts within a parent.
status:  live      — real content, written and reviewed
drafting  — partial content on the page
awaiting  — page exists, content not yet supplied
`needs` is what has to be handed over before the page can be written. It
doubles as the card text while status is `awaiting`, so a blank page never
pretends to be a finished one.
`body` names a file in projects/ to inline as the page content. Omit it and
build.py renders the standard skeleton from `sections`.
`embed` names a standalone HTML app in guides/ to inline as a
base64 payload and hydrate into a srcdoc iframe on first visit. The
page body must carry a matching <div class="gembed" data-guide="ID">.
Top-level nodes carry `track` (which of site.tracks they belong to) and
`phase` (their step in it). `flagship: true` marks the headline project.
sections: Who was stuck, on what, and why it mattered.
The actual work, in order, including what was tried and dropped.
Findings, decisions, shipped artifacts, numbers where there are numbers.
Scope held back deliberately, and the known soft spots.
The first thing the next person should do.

nodes.title: Hackathon
nodes.blurb: Sixteen hackathon projects scored on the same scale and sorted into build, test and park — each with an estimate from the person who wrote the code.
nodes.h1: Which sixteen hackathon projects deserve a roadmap slot?
nodes.lede: A hackathon produces enthusiasm, not a roadmap. This scores all sixteen on the same three things, merges the ones that were really the same idea, gets an estimate from each owner, and sorts them into four to build now, five to test first, and five to park with a way back.

nodes.title: Customer Intelligence
nodes.blurb: Three projects, one question: how do we tell a customer something true about their own fundraising that they could not work out alone? Two of them ran separately and found the same gap.
nodes.lede: What customers said they need, what the market already claims to sell, and a working answer to the gap both pointed at.

nodes.title: Fundraising Benchmarking
nodes.blurb: Puts every nonprofit next to organizations genuinely like it — same cause, same size — scores it, and turns the shortfall into a short list of things to try. 3,161 accounts, 38 peer groups.
nodes.h1: How is this organization really doing?
nodes.lede: Every nonprofit raises a different amount for different reasons. This compares each one against organizations genuinely like it, then turns the difference into a short list of what to try next.

nodes.title: Competitive Intelligence
nodes.blurb: Nine competitors, eight AI launches in twelve months, every claim graded on its evidence. All nine now promise trust. Not one offers proof.
nodes.h1: What nine competitors ship, claim, and never mention
nodes.lede: Every vendor now says it has AI, so the marketing tells you nothing. This separates what has actually shipped from what was only announced, puts every launch on one timeline, and grades the evidence behind each claim.

nodes.title: Audit & Gap Analysis
nodes.blurb: The claim-by-claim audit behind the scan: nine vendors, six capabilities, every cell graded, and the four gaps nobody has taken.
nodes.h1: What nine vendors claim, and what can be verified
nodes.lede: The workbook behind the scan. Every capability is graded shipped, claimed but unproven, or nowhere to be found — so you can tell a real feature from a press release.

nodes.title: Customer Interview Synthesis
nodes.blurb: 39 interviews across 33 organizations. They do not want more AI — they want AI they can control, understand and check. Reporting turned out to be the biggest source of pain.
nodes.h1: What 39 admins said about AI, reporting and insights
nodes.lede: Everyone agreed customers want AI. Nobody could say which AI, or why the AI we had already shipped was going unused. This pulls 39 interviews into one place and looks for what repeats.

nodes.title: Instrumentation
nodes.blurb: Two layers of measurement: a scoreboard for whether Pro is healthy, and an early-warning layer across eight parts of the product where every measure names the decision it would change.
nodes.h1: How would we know if the admin experience got better?
nodes.lede: Pro measured logins and revenue, which tells you the score after the month ends. There was also no agreed definition of an “active admin”, so two people could pull activation numbers from the same database and both be right.

nodes.title: UTM
nodes.blurb: Marketing tags were being dropped between the ad and the donation, so nonprofits could not tell which campaign raised the money. Twelve tickets, two leaks found and fixed, and five statuses that had moved since the slide was drawn.
nodes.h1: Making UTM survive the whole donation stack
nodes.lede: A UTM tag is the label a marketer puts on a link so they can tell which ad brought in a donation. GoFundMe Pro was losing them. This maps the whole programme, with every ticket status checked against Jira rather than copied off the slide.

nodes.title: Guides
nodes.blurb: Two attempts to leave something behind that works without me: one maps 1,202 code repositories, one turns 24 engineering requirements into questions a product manager can ask.
nodes.lede: Written so the next person does not have to work all this out again, and honest enough about their own limits to be safe to trust.

nodes.title: Non-Functional Guide
nodes.blurb: The 24 things that decide whether a release survives real users, each with the questions to ask engineering and the wording to put in the spec. Plus a 53-item launch checklist.
nodes.h1: The qualities that decide whether a release survives production
nodes.lede: A working feature answers “what does it do?” Everything that decides whether it holds up — speed, reliability, safety, and how expensive it is to change later — sits in a vocabulary most product managers were never taught. This is the translation.

nodes.title: Data Architecture Repo Guide
nodes.blurb: 1,202 code repositories sorted into ten groups, four journeys traced end to end, and a tool for “something broke, where do I look?” Every owner labeled documented, guessed or disputed.
nodes.h1: Where do I look, in 1,202 repositories?
nodes.lede: A product manager gets told something is broken and faces 1,202 repositories with no map. This is that map. It is built from repository data rather than from anyone's knowledge, and it says so on every screen.

nodes.title: Corporate Strategy
nodes.blurb: Two gaps in how GoFundMe grows, and five findings that size them — checked against the data rather than taken on faith.
nodes.lede: The growth argument underneath everything else here. Both gaps are the same problem: the platform is good at collecting from moments of generosity and bad at creating generous people.

nodes.title: How to Grow GDV
nodes.blurb: 20% of donors give 39% of the money, and half of that comes from people who gave exactly twice — not from the loyal regulars. Plus what one more gift is worth.
nodes.lede: Repeat donors are 20% of donors and 39% of the money. Most of that sits with people who gave twice, not with the loyal few.

nodes.title: How Do We Acquire Better Donors?
nodes.blurb: A better donor is one who gives again. Today 12.3% do, within about 23 days — and each extra percentage point is worth roughly $36M a year.
nodes.h1: How do we acquire better donors?
nodes.lede: A better donor is one who gives again. A second gift nearly doubles what they are worth in a year, and you can measure it in 90 days instead of waiting twelve months.

nodes.title: How Do We Build Better Relationships With Super Donors?
nodes.blurb: Four ideas aimed at the second gift: give the group an owner, email them in the three weeks that matter, get some of them in a room, and give them a yearly recap.
nodes.h1: How do we build better relationships with super donors?
nodes.lede: 7.1 million people give 39% of the money and get exactly the same experience as a first-time donor. The programme belongs at the second gift, where 4.9 million people and $871M already sit.

nodes.title: How Do We Make Giving Cool?
nodes.blurb: Donors who arrive through a message or a shared link come back at 27–28%. Donors who arrive through a social post come back at 10.6%, below average. The answer is getting people in a room together.
nodes.h1: How do we make giving cool?
nodes.lede: Coolness has to be borrowed from somewhere. The obvious source is fame. The data points somewhere else — at the people you already know.
